While these factors continue to explain much of the above-target inflation subsequently, residual cost push factors also contributed upward inflationary pressures, especially in the first quarter of 2022.","locator":"page 81","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, MAC-010","period_fit":"Direct fit: 2021-22 analysis period matches question 5B.9 shock context","source_limitations":["Philips curve estimation excludes pandemic period; conclusions broadly robust across different specifications"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0003","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The FEIP stabilization fund was nearly depleted after pandemic response, with MEX$157 billion transferred to the budget in 2020 leaving a balance of only MEX$9.5 billion (0.04% of GDP) against an assessed adequate balance of MEX$100 billion (0.35% of GDP).","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"FEIP (Fondo de Estabilización de los Ingresos Presupuestarios)","action":"fund depletion via budget transfer during pandemic","mechanism":"revenue shortfall relative to budget projections","outcome":"FEIP balance fell from MEX$158 billion (0.6% GDP) to MEX$9.5 billion (0.04% GDP) by end-2020, creating insufficient fiscal contingency","dates":["2020","end-2020"],"quantities":["MEX$157 billion transferred to budget","MEX$9.5 billion balance (0.04% of GDP)","MEX$100 billion adequate target (0.35% of GDP)","MEX$158 billion prior balance (0.6% of GDP)"],"excerpt":"FEIP transferred a total of MEX$157 billion (0.7 percent of GDP) to the budget due to revenue shortfalls relative to budget projections. The balance of the fund marked MEX$9.5 billion (0.04 percent of GDP) by the end-2020 compared to MEX$158 billion (0.6 percent of GDP) in the previous year.","locator":"page 84","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, MAC-010","period_fit":"Strong fit: 2020 depletion directly precedes and constrains 2023 fiscal response capacity","source_limitations":["FEIP balance MEX$25 billion (0.09% GDP) as of end-June 2022 per subsequent paragraph; expected 2022 transfers only 0.03% GDP additional"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0004","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's current fiscal framework contains a Balanced-Budget Rule and a Public Sector Borrowing Requirement Rule that are broadly pro-cyclical, limiting fiscal policy flexibility to respond to economic shocks.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican fiscal framework","action":"pro-cyclical fiscal rules constraining policy flexibility","mechanism":"Balanced-Budget Rule (BBR) and Public Sector Borrowing Requirement Rule (PSBR)","outcome":"Framework deemed pro-cyclical; escape clauses were used only 7 of 13 years to 2020, indicating chronic inflexibility","dates":["2010-2012","2014-2016","to 2020"],"quantities":["7 of 13 years escape clauses used","6 escape clause triggers in current framework"],"excerpt":"The Balanced-Budget Rule (BBR) requires that the budget must be balanced on a cash basis. The rule is broadly procyclical. The Public Sector Borrowing Requirement Rule (PSBR) requires that the budget documentation sets a target for the public sector borrowing requirement. Escape clauses were used in 2010-12 and 2014-16, meaning that the framework was only respected in 7 out of the 13 years to 2020.","locator":"page 87","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, MAC-010","period_fit":"Strong fit: pro-cyclical framework directly relevant to fiscal policy credibility and shock response under 5B.3 and 5B.9","source_limitations":["Staff characterization; reform proposals based on this assessment; actual escape clause usage depends on political and economic conditions"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0005","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The 2023 budget package proposed reforms allowing FEIP financing via government IOUs when debt issuance falls short of the budget ceiling, enabling FEIP to hold financial assets without incurring liabilities, expected to free up MEX$20-30 billion.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government","action":"proposing fiscal framework reform to expand FEIP financing mechanisms","mechanism":"government IOUs deposited in FEIP when actual debt issuance is below ceiling","outcome":"Enables FEIP to hold financial assets (not just cash) without incurring liabilities; expected to free up MEX$20-30 billion for contingency","dates":["2023 budget package"],"quantities":["MEX$20-30 billion expected to be freed up"],"excerpt":"Reforms to the FRBL proposed in the government's 2023 budget package would create a new funding mechanism for FEIP based on debt issuance. Under the proposals, where actual debt issuance falls short of that budgeted for the year, the government would create an IOU equivalent to the shortfall between actual debt issuance and the debt ceiling in the budget and deposit this in FEIP. The reforms enable FEIP to hold financial assets, though it still cannot incur financial liabilities.","locator":"page 85","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, MAC-010","period_fit":"Strong fit: 2023 reform directly addresses fiscal contingency replenishment relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9","source_limitations":["Reforms trade-offs: complexity increases; additional funding unpredictable and predicated on headroom against debt ceiling; does not address pro-cyclical bias"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0006","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Philips curve estimation for Mexico shows approximately equal weights on expected inflation (~0.52) and lagged inflation (~0.48) for headline inflation, confirming backward-looking inflation dynamics that last relatively longer than in advanced economies.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexico's inflation process","action":"inflation persistence via backward-looking dynamics","mechanism":"hybrid Philips curve with equal weights on expected (0.52) and lagged (0.48) inflation","outcome":"Past inflation shocks contribute to current dynamics for relatively longer in Mexico vs advanced economies; relatively higher inflation volatility","dates":[],"quantities":["0.52 weight on expected inflation","0.48 weight on lagged inflation","R² 0.75-0.77 for headline inflation"],"excerpt":"The results presented in the table suggest roughly equal weights in the case of headline inflation (0.52 versus. 0.48). This result is broadly in line with the conventional view of a relatively greater role of past inflation in contributing to current inflation dynamics in Mexico and other emerging market economies compared to advanced economies.","locator":"page 82","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, MAC-010","period_fit":"Strong fit: backward-looking inflation dynamics directly relevant to 2021-22 surge and monetary policy effectiveness under 5B.3","source_limitations":["Core inflation R² only 0.33-0.34, indicating standard determinants explain relatively less of core variation; estimation excludes pandemic period"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0007","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's fiscal contingencies remained low while downside risks were rising; FEIP balance was MEX$25.0 billion (0.09% of 2022 GDP) as of end-June 2022 against an assessed adequacy threshold of MEX$100 billion (0.35% of 2022 GDP), leaving a significant gap.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"FEIP","action":"inadequate fiscal contingency balance","mechanism":"low FEIP balance relative to adequacy threshold","outcome":"Fiscal buffer severely below adequate level while downside risks to global and Mexican economies were rising for 2023","dates":["end-June 2022","2023"],"quantities":["MEX$25.0 billion FEIP balance (0.09% of 2022 GDP)","MEX$100 billion adequacy threshold (0.35% of 2022 GDP)"],"excerpt":"the balance in the fund was MEX$25.0 billion (0.09 percent of 2022 GDP) as of end-June 2022 and the aforementioned expected transfers to the fund in 2022 will only provide an additional 0.03 percent of GDP.
